s0003.literal: Founder Empress Zhang; Emperor Wen Empress Shen; Deposed Emperor Empress Wang; Emperor Xuan Empress Liu
s0003.idiomatic: Founder Empress Zhang; Emperor Wen Empress Shen; Deposed Emperor Empress Wang; Emperor Xuan Empress Liu

s0004.literal: Last Emperor Empress Shen; Noble Consort Zhang
s0004.idiomatic: Last Emperor Empress Shen; Noble Consort Zhang

s0005.literal: In the Rites of Zhou, the king establishes a queen, the Six Palaces, three consorts, nine concubines, twenty-seven secondary wives, and eighty-one attendant wives to hear and govern inner affairs throughout the realm.
s0005.idiomatic: The Rites of Zhou say that a king establishes a queen, the Six Palaces, three chief consorts, nine concubines, twenty-seven secondary wives, and eighty-one attendant wives to govern the inner realm.

s0006.literal: Yet rulers who receive the Mandate and succeed to the line are aided not only by ministers without; surely inner virtue assists as well.
s0006.idiomatic: Yet rulers who receive the Mandate and succeed to the throne are aided not only by ministers without, but also by virtue within.

s0007.literal: From Han and Wei onward the offices of the Six Palaces were inherited and increased, and each age differed.
s0007.idiomatic: From Han and Wei onward the offices of the Six Palaces were carried on and expanded, and no two dynasties were alike.

s0008.literal: The Founder received the succession amid turmoil and disorder and brightly bore Heaven's calendar; because he kept himself in plain simplicity, many posts in the inner palace stood vacant.
s0008.idiomatic: The Founder took the throne amid turmoil and lived plainly, so many posts in the inner palace went unfilled.

s0009.literal: In the first year of Tianjia under Emperor Wen, an edict fixed the number of inner-palace posts; for the first time three offices were established—noble consort, noble concubine, and noble lady—to match the ancient three consorts.
s0009.idiomatic: In Tianjia year 1 (562) Emperor Wen fixed the number of inner-palace posts and for the first time created three offices—noble consort, noble concubine, and noble lady—to match the ancient three chief consorts.

s0010.literal: There were also established nine persons: Shuyuan, Shuyi, Shurong, Zhaohua, Zhaorong, Zhaoyi, Editorial footnote marker 1. Xiuhua, Xiuyi, and Xiurong, to match the ancient nine concubines.
s0010.idiomatic: He also appointed nine women—Shuyuan, Shuyi, Shurong, Zhaohua, Zhaorong, Zhaoyi, [1] Xiuhua, Xiuyi, and Xiurong—to match the ancient nine concubines.

s0011.literal: There were also established five offices—Jieyu, Ronghua, Chonghua, Chenghui, and Lierong—called the Five Duties, ranking below the nine concubines.
s0011.idiomatic: He also created five offices—Jieyu, Ronghua, Chonghua, Chenghui, and Lierong—the Five Duties, ranking below the nine concubines.

s0012.literal: There were also established three offices—Beauty, Talent, and Good Wife—with no fixed quota for their posts; they were called scattered ranks.
s0012.idiomatic: He also created three offices—Beauty, Talent, and Good Wife—with no fixed quota; they were called scattered ranks.

s0013.literal: Emperor Wen was by nature respectful and frugal, yet many concubines' posts still stood vacant; Emperor Xuan and the Last Emperor made no changes to the inner offices.
s0013.idiomatic: Emperor Wen was respectful and frugal, and many concubines' posts still went unfilled; Emperor Xuan and the Last Emperor changed nothing in the inner offices.

s0015.literal: [Now] what is compiled here, Editorial footnote marker 2. briefly supplies this chapter.
s0015.idiomatic: [Now] what is compiled here [2] briefly supplies this chapter.

s0017.literal: The Founder's Empress Xuan, of the Zhang clan, personal name Yaor, was a native of Wucheng in Wuxing.
s0017.idiomatic: Lady Xuan, empress of the Founder, of the Zhang clan, was named Yaor and came from Wucheng in Wuxing.

s0018.literal: Her original surname was Niu; her father Jingming was adopted by the Zhang clan and therefore changed it.
s0018.idiomatic: Her family had borne the surname Niu; her father Jingming was adopted by the Zhang clan and took their name.

s0019.literal: Jingming under Liang reached the office of scattered-cavalry gentleman.
s0019.idiomatic: Jingming had served Liang as scattered-cavalry gentleman.

s0020.literal: The empress's mother Su once met a Daoist who gave her a small turtle with a five-colored radiance, saying, "In three years there will be a sign."
s0020.idiomatic: The empress's mother Su once met a Daoist who gave her a small turtle glowing in five colors and said, "In three years there will be a sign."

s0021.literal: When the term arrived, the empress was born and purple light filled the chamber; the turtle's whereabouts were then lost.
s0021.idiomatic: When the time came, the empress was born and purple light filled the room; the turtle was nowhere to be found.

s0022.literal: In youth she was clever and quick, with a beautiful bearing; her fingernails were five inches long, reddish and white in color, and whenever there were mourning garments that hindered work, one nail would break first.
s0022.idiomatic: As a girl she was clever and beautiful; her fingernails were five inches long, reddish white, and whenever she wore mourning garments that got in the way, one nail would snap first.

s0023.literal: The Founder first married a daughter of Qian Zhongfang of the same commandery, who died early; afterward he betrothed the empress.
s0023.idiomatic: The Founder had first married a daughter of Qian Zhongfang of the same commandery, who died young; only then did he betroth the empress.

s0024.literal: The empress was skilled at writing and reckoning and could recite the Odes and the Songs of Chu.
s0024.idiomatic: The empress was skilled at writing and reckoning and could recite the Odes and the Songs of Chu.

s0025.literal: When the Founder from Guangzhou campaigned south against Jiaozhi, he ordered the empress to follow Prince of Hengyang Chang with Emperor Wen by the sea route back to Changcheng.
s0025.idiomatic: When the Founder marched from Guangzhou against Jiaozhi, he sent the empress with Prince of Hengyang Chang and Emperor Wen home by sea to Changcheng.

s0026.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion the Founder went down to Yuzhang; the empress was imprisoned by Jing.
s0026.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion the Founder went down to Yuzhang, and the empress was taken prisoner by Jing.

s0027.literal: When Jing was pacified and the Founder became Duke of Changcheng county, the empress was invested as Lady.
s0027.idiomatic: After Jing fell and the Founder became Duke of Changcheng, the empress was made his lady.

s0028.literal: When the Founder ascended the throne, in the first year of Yongding she was established as empress.
s0028.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, in Yongding year 1 (557) she was made empress.

s0029.literal: The empress's father Jingming was posthumously promoted to special grand master and grand master with golden seal and purple ribbon, with a golden seal and purple cord added; the empress's mother Su was invested as Lady of Anji county.
s0029.idiomatic: The empress's father Jingming was posthumously made special grand master and grand master with the gold seal and purple ribbon; her mother Su was made Lady of Anji county.

s0030.literal: In the second year the Lady of Anji died and was buried with the empress's father in Wuxing.
s0030.idiomatic: In the second year the Lady of Anji died and was buried with the empress's father in Wuxing.

s0031.literal: The next year the empress's father was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Guangde county with a fief of five hundred households; his posthumous title was Wen.
s0031.idiomatic: The next year her father was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Guangde with five hundred households; his posthumous title was Wen.

s0032.literal: When the Founder died, the empress with Masters of Writing Attendant Cai Jingli settled the plan, kept the death secret, and summoned Emperor Wen to succeed; the matter is in the biographies of Cai Jingli and Hou Andu.
s0032.idiomatic: When the Founder died, the empress and masters of writing attendant Cai Jingli laid their plans, kept the death secret, and summoned Emperor Wen to succeed; the affair is told in the biographies of Cai Jingli and Hou Andu.

s0033.literal: When Emperor Wen took the throne, the empress was honored as empress dowager; her palace was called Cixun.
s0033.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded, the empress was honored as empress dowager; her palace was called Cixun.

s0034.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, the empress was honored as grand empress dowager.
s0034.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne, she was honored as grand empress dowager.

s0035.literal: In the second year of Guangda the empress issued an order deposing the Deposed Emperor as Prince of Linhai and appointing Emperor Xuan to succeed.
s0035.idiomatic: In Guangda year 2 (569) she issued an order deposing the Deposed Emperor as Prince of Linhai and installing Emperor Xuan in his place.

s0036.literal: In the first year of Taijian she was again honored as empress dowager.
s0036.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 (569) she was again honored as empress dowager.

s0037.literal: In the second year, third month, day renshen, she died in the Hall of Purple Apex at age sixty-five.
s0037.idiomatic: In the third month of Taijian year 2 (570), on day renshen, she died in the Hall of Purple Apex at sixty-five.

s0038.literal: Her final command was that all funeral needs be kept frugal and simple, and that offerings presented at the mourning must not use oxen or sheep.
s0038.idiomatic: Her last command was that the funeral be kept frugal and that no offerings of oxen or sheep be used.

s0039.literal: That year, fourth month, the ministers submitted the posthumous title Empress Dowager Xuan; she was buried with the Founder at Wan'an Mausoleum.
s0039.idiomatic: That fourth month the ministers gave her the posthumous title Empress Dowager Xuan; she was buried with the Founder at Wan'an Mausoleum.

s0040.literal: None of the empress's close kin held office at court; only a clansman of the same surname, Niu Zhi, reached the post of palace gentleman of the central staff.
s0040.idiomatic: None of the empress's close kin held office at court; only a clansman, Niu Zhi, rose to palace gentleman of the central staff.

s0042.literal: Emperor Wen's Empress Shen, personal name Miaorong, was a native of Wukang in Wuxing.
s0042.idiomatic: Emperor Wen's empress Shen, named Miaorong, came from Wukang in Wuxing.

s0043.literal: Her father Fashen under Liang was recorder of the Prince of An's front headquarters.
s0043.idiomatic: Her father Fashen had served Liang as recorder of the Prince of An's front headquarters.

s0044.literal: When the empress was a little more than ten years old, in the Datong era of Liang she was married to Emperor Wen.
s0044.idiomatic: When she was barely ten, in the Datong era of Liang she was married to Emperor Wen.

s0045.literal: When the Founder campaigned against Hou Jing, Emperor Wen was then in Wuxing; Jing sent envoys to seize Emperor Wen and the empress.
s0045.idiomatic: When the Founder moved against Hou Jing, Emperor Wen was in Wuxing; Jing sent men to seize him and the empress.

s0046.literal: When Jing was pacified, they were then released.
s0046.idiomatic: After Jing fell they were freed.

s0047.literal: When the Founder ascended the throne, in the first year of Yongding the empress became Princess of Linchuan.
s0047.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, in Yongding year 1 (557) she became Princess of Linchuan.

s0048.literal: When Emperor Wen took the throne, she became empress.
s0048.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded, she was made empress.

s0049.literal: The empress's father Fashen was posthumously promoted to grand master with golden seal and purple ribbon and enfeoffed as Marquis of Jian
s0049.idiomatic: Her father Fashen was posthumously made grand master with the gold seal and purple ribbon and enfeoffed as Marquis of Jian

s0051.literal: [cheng] county, Editorial footnote marker 3. fief five hundred households, posthumous title Gong; the empress's mother Gao was posthumously invested as Lady of Anji county, posthumous title Ding.
s0051.idiomatic: [cheng] county, [3] with a fief of five hundred households and posthumous title Gong; her mother Gao was posthumously made Lady of Anji county with posthumous title Ding.

s0052.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, the empress was honored as empress dowager; her palace was called Ande.
s0052.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne, she was honored as empress dowager; her palace was called Ande.

s0053.literal: At that time Emperor Xuan, together with Vice Director Dao Zhongju, Attendant Liu Shizhi, and others, all received the testament and assisted in government; Shizhi and Zhongju constantly dwelt within the forbidden quarters deciding military affairs, while Emperor Xuan was Inspector of Yangzhou and entered the Masters of Writing office with three hundred followers.
s0053.idiomatic: At that time Emperor Xuan, with vice director Dao Zhongju, attendant Liu Shizhi, and others, shared the testament and governed; Shizhi and Zhongju lived in the inner palace and decided affairs of state, while Emperor Xuan was inspector of Yangzhou and lodged in the masters of writing office with three hundred men.

s0054.literal: Shizhi saw Emperor Xuan's power growing and secretly resented him; he therefore forged an order and told Emperor Xuan, "Now the four quarters are at peace; Your Highness may return to the Eastern Mansion and manage the prefecture's affairs."
s0054.idiomatic: Shizhi saw Emperor Xuan's power growing and secretly feared him; he forged an order saying, "The realm is at peace; you may return to the Eastern Mansion and mind the prefecture."

s0055.literal: Emperor Xuan was about to go out when Adviser Mao Xi stopped him and said, "If you go out now you will be subject to others—as with Cao Shuang, you may wish to be a rich householder yet cannot obtain it."
s0055.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan was about to leave when adviser Mao Xi stopped him and said, "Go out now and you fall under another's hand—as with Cao Shuang, you may wish only to be a rich man and cannot even have that."

s0056.literal: Emperor Xuan then claimed illness, summoned Shizhi and detained him to talk, and sent Mao Xi in first to speak to the empress.
s0056.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan then feigned illness, summoned Shizhi and kept him talking, and sent Mao Xi ahead to speak to the empress.

s0057.literal: The empress said, "Now Bozong is young; all government is entrusted to the Second Lord—this is not my wish."
s0057.idiomatic: The empress said, "Bozong is still young; to put all government in the Second Lord's hands is not my wish."

s0058.literal: Xi also spoke to the Deposed Emperor; the emperor said, "This was done by Shizhi and the others alone; it is not my wish."
s0058.idiomatic: Xi also spoke to the Deposed Emperor, who said, "That was Shizhi and his party—not my wish."

s0059.literal: Xi went out and reported to Emperor Xuan; Emperor Xuan therefore imprisoned Shizhi, entered in person to see the empress and the emperor, set forth Shizhi's faults at length, himself drafted the edict and requested the seal, and handed Shizhi over to the Court of Trials for punishment.
s0059.idiomatic: Xi came out and told Emperor Xuan, who then seized Shizhi, went in to see the empress and the emperor, laid out Shizhi's crimes, drafted the edict himself, and sent Shizhi to the court of trials.

s0060.literal: That night he was granted death in prison.
s0060.idiomatic: That night he was granted death in prison.

s0061.literal: From then on, whether affairs were great or small, all fell to Emperor Xuan.
s0061.idiomatic: From then on, great and small alike, all power passed to Emperor Xuan.

s0062.literal: The empress, worried and distressed with no plan, secretly bribed the eunuch Jiang Yu to induce Zhang Anguo of Jian'an to hold the commandery in rebellion, hoping thereby to strike at Emperor Xuan.
s0062.idiomatic: The empress, anxious and at her wits' end, secretly bribed the eunuch Jiang Yu to stir Zhang Anguo of Jian'an into holding the commandery in rebellion, hoping thus to move against Emperor Xuan.

s0063.literal: When Anguo's affair was discovered, all were executed by Emperor Xuan.
s0063.idiomatic: When Anguo's plot was discovered, Emperor Xuan had them all executed.

s0064.literal: At that time the empress's close attendants largely knew of the affair; fearing that their associates would be seized together, she had them all killed.
s0064.idiomatic: Her close attendants largely knew of the plot; fearing they would be seized with their associates, she had them all killed.

s0065.literal: When Emperor Xuan took the throne, the empress was made Empress Wen.
s0065.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan succeeded, the empress was titled Empress Wen.

s0066.literal: When Chen fell and entered Sui, in the early Daye era she returned from Chang'an to the southland; before long she died.
s0066.idiomatic: When Chen fell to Sui, in the early Daye era she returned from Chang'an to the south; soon she died.

s0067.literal: The empress's elder brother Qin followed Emperor Wen on campaign and for merit reached the post of steadfast-prestige general and Inspector of Anzhou.
s0067.idiomatic: The empress's elder brother Qin followed Emperor Wen on campaign and for merit rose to steadfast-prestige general and inspector of Anzhou.

s0068.literal: When Emperor Wen took the throne, [Qin] inherited the enfeoffment as Marquis of Jiancheng, was promoted to supernumerary regular attendant for direct communication, given credentials, made area commander of the nine commanderies including Kuaiji, bright-prestige general, and Kuaiji Administrator; he entered court as palace attendant, left guard general, and guard commandant.
s0068.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded, Qin inherited the marquisate of Jiancheng, was made supernumerary regular attendant for direct communication with credentials, area commander of nine commanderies including Kuaiji, bright-prestige general, and Kuaiji administrator, then entered court as palace attendant, left guard general, and guard commandant.

s0069.literal: In the Guangda era he was right vice director of the masters of writing; soon he was transferred to left vice director.
s0069.idiomatic: In the Guangda era he was right vice director of the masters of writing, then left vice director.

s0070.literal: Qin by nature had no skill; he looked only to his own comfort.
s0070.idiomatic: Qin had no talent and cared only for his own ease.

s0071.literal: When Emperor Xuan took the throne, [Qin] went out as cloud-banner general and Administrator of Yixing, salary at two thousand shi of the middle rank.
s0071.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan succeeded, Qin went out as cloud-banner general and administrator of Yixing at two thousand shi of the middle rank.

s0072.literal: In the first year of Taijian he died at age sixty-seven; he was posthumously given palace attendant, special grand master, and left assistant general, posthumous title Cheng.
s0072.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 (569) he died at sixty-seven; he was posthumously made palace attendant, special grand master, and left assistant general, with posthumous title Cheng.

s0073.literal: His son Guan succeeded him; he had considerable learning and reached the post of imperial censor.
s0073.idiomatic: His son Guan succeeded him; Guan was learned and rose to imperial censor.

s0075.literal: The Deposed Emperor's Empress Wang was a daughter of Grand Master with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon Gu.
s0075.idiomatic: The Deposed Emperor's empress Wang was a daughter of grand master with the gold seal and purple ribbon Gu.

s0076.literal: In the first year of Tianjia she became crown princess; when the Deposed Emperor took the throne she was established as empress.
s0076.idiomatic: In Tianjia year 1 (562) she became crown princess; when the Deposed Emperor succeeded she was made empress.

s0077.literal: When the Deposed Emperor became Prince of Linhai, the empress became Princess of Linhai.
s0077.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor was made Prince of Linhai, she became Princess of Linhai.

s0078.literal: In the Zhide era she died.
s0078.idiomatic: In the Zhide era she died.

s0080.literal: The empress was by nature modest and cautious; she never made requests on behalf of her clan, and even in food and clothing she gave them nothing.
s0080.idiomatic: The empress was modest and cautious; she never asked favors for her clan and shared neither food nor clothing with them.

s0081.literal: Her younger brother Pan in the Taijian era married Emperor Wen's daughter Princess of Fuyang and was appointed commandant of the emperor's son-in-law.
s0081.idiomatic: Her younger brother Pan in the Taijian era married Emperor Wen's daughter, Princess of Fuyang, and was made commandant of the emperor's son-in-law.

s0082.literal: When the Last Emperor took the throne, as the emperor's maternal uncle he was promoted to scattered-cavalry regular attendant.
s0082.idiomatic: When the Last Emperor succeeded, as the emperor's uncle by marriage he was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0083.literal: Pan was dull and foolish, fond of wine; he often rode his horse drunk through the palace gate and was impeached by the responsible offices, stripped of office, and died at home.
s0083.idiomatic: Pan was dull and fond of drink; drunk, he often rode through the palace gate, was impeached, dismissed, and died at home.

s0084.literal: He was posthumously given palace attendant and central guard commander.
s0084.idiomatic: He was posthumously made palace attendant and central guard commander.

s0086.literal: The empress had no son; she adopted Sun Ji's son Yin as her own child.
s0086.idiomatic: The empress had no son; she adopted Sun Ji's son Yin as her own.

s0087.literal: Many in the empress's clan held eminent office; the matter is in the biography of Junli.
s0087.idiomatic: Many of her clan held high office; their stories are in the biography of Junli.

s0088.literal: The empress's uncle Jun Gong, after Emperor Yuan of Liang was defeated, remained constantly at Jiangling.
s0088.idiomatic: Her uncle Jun Gong, after Emperor Yuan of Liang was defeated, stayed at Jiangling.

s0089.literal: In the Zhenming era, together with Xiao Kan and Xiao Yan he led their followers in defecting from Sui and returning to court; the Last Emperor promoted him to grand mentor of the heir apparent.
s0089.idiomatic: In the Zhenming era he and Xiao Kan and Xiao Yan led their men in defecting from Sui back to Chen; the Last Emperor made him grand mentor of the heir apparent.

s0090.literal: Jun Gong was broadly learned, talented in debate, and skilled at discussion; the Last Emperor valued him deeply.
s0090.idiomatic: Jun Gong was learned, eloquent, and skilled in debate; the Last Emperor prized him highly.

s0091.literal: When Chen fell, Emperor Wen of Sui, because he had rebelled against Sui, ordered him beheaded at Jiankang.
s0091.idiomatic: When Chen fell, Emperor Wen of Sui had him beheaded at Jiankang for rebelling against Sui.

s0092.literal: Last Emperor Noble Consort Zhang Lihua
s0092.idiomatic: Last Emperor Noble Consort Zhang Lihua

s0094.literal: The historiographer, Palace Attendant and Duke of Zheng, Wei Zheng, examined records and consulted elders, saying: When the Last Emperor first took the throne, because of the disorder of Prince of Shixing Shuling, he was wounded and lay ill below the Hall of Accepting Fragrance; at that time none of the ladies could enter—only Noble Consort Zhang attended him.
s0094.idiomatic: The historiographer, palace attendant and Duke of Zheng, Wei Zheng, examined the records and consulted elders and wrote: When the Last Emperor first succeeded, he was wounded in the disorder of Prince of Shixing Shuling and lay ill below the Hall of Accepting Fragrance; none of the palace women could enter—only Noble Consort Zhang attended him.

s0095.literal: Yet Empress Dowager Liu still dwelt in the Hall of Cypress Beam—that is, the empress's principal hall.
s0095.idiomatic: Yet Empress Dowager Liu still lived in the Hall of Cypress Beam, the empress's proper hall.

s0096.literal: The Last Emperor's Empress Shen had never been favored and could not attend his illness; she lived apart in the Hall of Seeking the Worthy.
s0096.idiomatic: The Last Emperor's empress Shen had never been favored and could not nurse him; she lived apart in the Hall of Seeking the Worthy.

s0097.literal: In the second year of Zhide, before the Hall of Radiant Light he raised the three towers Linchun, Jieqi, and Wangxian.
s0097.idiomatic: In Zhide year 2 (584) he raised the three towers Linchun, Jieqi, and Wangxian before the Hall of Radiant Light.

s0098.literal: Editorial footnote marker 7. The towers were several zhang high, with dozens of bays; their windows, wall bands, hanging lintels, and balustrades were all made of agarwood, further adorned with gold and jade and set with pearls and kingfisher feathers; outside hung pearl curtains, within were jeweled canopies and jeweled curtains; their garments and ornaments were marvelous and rare, unmatched in recent antiquity.
s0098.idiomatic: [7] The towers stood several zhang high, with dozens of bays. Windows, wall bands, lintels, and balustrades were all of agarwood, adorned with gold, jade, pearls, and kingfisher feathers; pearl curtains hung without, jeweled canopies within; their dress and ornaments were wonders such as recent ages had never seen.

s0099.literal: Whenever a slight breeze passed, the fragrance was smelled for several li; when the morning sun first shone, light flooded the rear court.
s0099.idiomatic: When a breeze stirred, the fragrance carried for miles; at first light the rear court blazed with radiance.

s0100.literal: Below they piled stone into mountains, led water into pools, planted strange trees, and mixed in flowers and herbs.
s0100.idiomatic: Below they piled stone into hills, led water into pools, and planted rare trees and flowers.
